title: Reading The Sky Raw
eyebrow: Every sky readout now ignores the camera, and three older faults surfaced behind it

questions.ask: The work is finished and on main. Two of the three faults it exposed block every sky measurement. Where do I go next?

options.label: Fix the two blockers
options.say: Take the two faults that block the sky measurements, in that order.
options.note: Medium. Until the readouts stop agreeing with each other at clear weather, and the control stops carrying the cloud it excludes, nothing about the sky can be measured against a law — the checks would only compare the app with itself, which is what we just stopped doing

options.label: Write the sky measurements now
options.say: Write the sky checks against the readouts as they are.
options.note: Faster to something on the screen, but four of them would rest on the two broken readouts and go green for the wrong reason

options.label: Leave the sky, go elsewhere
options.say: Park the sky; the three faults stay on the board.
options.note: Costs nothing today. The three are recorded with the runs that found them, so picking them up later is cheap

questions.note: All three faults are older than this change and none is caused by it.

content.label: The picture you asked for
content.lead: How much sky shows through the cloud. Same circuit, same weather, camera pointed up, read the old way and the new way.

before.caption: Before: white, and white again wherever you look

after.caption: After: a picture with values in it, from 0.06 to 0.69

blocks.label: The old one is not a dim picture that needs turning up
blocks.text: It is a reading of nearly all of it, nearly everywhere — the answer a cloudless sky would give, in weather that is six-tenths covered. The new one carries a range, and every pixel of it is the number itself.

content.label: Before and after, same command
content.lead: Camera aimed at the sky over a circuit, cloud in the frame. Moved is the share of the sky that changes when brightening moves by one stop, which for a real readout must be nothing. Spread is darkest to brightest: a readout with no spread is carrying no information.

rows: How much shows through the cloud
The overcast law on its own

blocks.label: Both targets met
blocks.text: Not one pixel of any readout responds to brightening now, against 99.4% at worst before. Eleven were pinned at pure white and none is. Repeat noise fell to nothing as well, because a readout no longer joins the frame-blending path.

content.label: Three older faults the clean readouts exposed
content.lead: None is caused by this change. All three were invisible while everything read white, and all three are now on the board.

rows.title: With no cloud at all, every sky readout shows the same picture
rows.note: It is worse than it first looked. Given eight seconds to settle with the weather at zero, all thirteen readouts land on one of only two answers, each agreeing to three digits. None of them is showing its own quantity; they are showing the ordinary sky, in two flavours. Put a deck back and they separate. This is the same thing an earlier note recorded as the cloud readouts being 'non-empty' with no cloud, and it kills the cleanest test the sky has: with no cloud, the cloud terms must be zero.

rows.title: The readout meant to have the cloud taken out still has the cloud in it
rows.note: One of the thirteen is the control: the sky as it would be with the cloud step removed, which is what every cloud term would be judged against. At six-tenths cover it carries crisp cloud shapes. Switch the cloud off and the same readout is a smooth gradient, so the shapes are the cloud — 84% of its pixels move. A control that carries what it is controlling for is worse than no control.

rows.title: A reading taken two seconds after the weather changes has not settled
rows.note: Wait four times as long and the figures move, while two captures inside one run agree perfectly. So the sky is still converging, not wobbling. It also depends on what ran before it: the same weather read differently after a run at clear weather than from a fresh start. A number that depends on how long you waited cannot carry a law, so the wait has to be replaced by waiting for the sky to say it is finished — which it already announces.

blocks.label: What this means for the sky measurements
blocks.text: The first blocks the cleanest test outright and the second removes the control the rest would be judged against. The sky checks wait on those two, not on this change.

content.label: What a readout is supposed to be
content.lead: Instead of the normal picture, the app can paint one measured quantity across the frame. Every part of the renderer has these, and in every part except one the pixel is the number itself.

rows.title: Everywhere else, the camera is switched off for a readout
rows.note: Brightening, the sensor, the film curve, the lens — all of it stands down, so what reaches the screen is the raw quantity. That is what lets a measurement say a number is right, rather than that a picture changed.

rows.title: The sky keeps the camera on, on purpose
rows.note: The thirteen sky readouts run through the full camera, and their values are pre-divided by how bright the clear sky happens to be so that brightening lands them somewhere visible. The reasoning is written into the code as a deliberate choice.

rows.title: So the sky is the one place a number cannot be read
rows.note: Three unknowns sit between the quantity and the pixel. Measured consequence: how much sky shows through the cloud reads a flat maximum at every weather setting, which is not a reading, and four attempted sky measurements could only compare the app against itself.

content.label: What changes
content.lead: The sky joins every other band. Camera off for a sky readout, and the divide-by-clear-sky dropped, because it only existed to survive the camera.

rows.title: The sky's laws become checkable at all
rows.note: Light through cloud between none and all of it, and falling as the path lengthens. Sun-lit cloud plus sky-lit cloud adding back to the whole cloud. The sun disc covering its published patch of sky. None of these can be read off a curved picture.

rows.title: The readouts become comparable with each other
rows.note: Two sky quantities can be held against one another only if both are on the same scale. Dividing each by the weather of the moment took that away.

rows.title: The normal picture is untouched
rows.note: This only affects what happens when a sky readout is selected. Nothing on the path to an ordinary photograph moves.

blocks.label: Not in scope
blocks.text: The readouts that show what one camera stage did to a photograph keep the camera on, because there a photograph is the thing being measured.

content.label: Half of them cannot fit in a picture at all
content.lead: Looking closely at the thirteen split them in two, and only one half is fixed by taking the camera away.

rows: Quantities that already sit between none and all — how much shows through the cloud, how much survives the air, how much sun reaches the deck, where cloud exists, how far away it is
Take the camera away and stop multiplying by the weather. Then the picture is the number, exactly.
Brightnesses, which have no ceiling — the cloud's own light, the light the air adds, the clear sky, the two halves of what lights a cloud, the two amounts falling on the deck
A picture holds 256 shades per colour and stops at white. A daylight sky runs thousands of times past that ceiling, so no honest picture of it exists.

blocks.label: Why that matters more than it sounds
blocks.text: The law you care most about — a cloud lit by sun plus the same cloud lit by sky adding back to the whole cloud — lives entirely in the second half. Squeezing those into a picture means dividing them by a number somebody made up, which is the exact habit we just agreed to stop.

blocks.label: So they are read before they become a picture
blocks.text: The sky is worked out in full precision before it is ever shown. That store can already be read back in real brightness units, and it is the same store the picture is drawn from — so the second half is measured there, at full precision, rather than after it has been flattened.

content.label: What stops it coming back
content.lead: A standing check now reads all thirteen every time the suite runs, and holds each one to three things.

rows.title: Brightening moves nothing
rows.note: Two captures a stop apart, identical pixel for pixel.

rows.title: The same readout twice gives the same answer
rows.note: Two captures with nothing changed between them, identical pixel for pixel.

rows.title: The middle reading is not at the top of the range
rows.note: A readout pinned at the maximum is carrying no information, which is exactly how this fault looked.

blocks.label: Proved by putting the fault back
blocks.text: With the old delivery restored the check goes red on every one of the thirteen: the whole sky moves under a stop of brightening and three readouts sit at the maximum again. It reads the list of thirteen off the app itself, so a fourteenth is covered the day it is added.

blocks.label: Read by someone who did not write it, and written down
blocks.text: An independent read of the change found nothing. The sky's own notes now say what a readout hands over, that the seven brightness ones cannot be read off a screen at all, and that the control and the null test are unavailable until the two faults above are fixed — so the next person does not build a measurement on either.

content.label: How it was judged
content.lead: The three things you asked to see, and what each one came back as.

rows.title: A stop of brightening must not move the picture — met
rows.note: Two captures of each of the thirteen, one stop apart, identical pixel for pixel. Before, the worst moved 99.4% of the sky.

rows.title: A sky readout must show a spread, bounded — met
rows.note: How much of a cloud's own light survives the air reads 0.08 to 0.44 where it read a flat 1.00. Eleven of the thirteen were pinned at the maximum and none is.

rows.title: One picture, before and after — at the top of this page
rows.note: Same circuit, same weather, one build at the commit before the change and one after.

decisions.title: A readout shows raw values, with no exception for the sky
decisions.why: Your words: the panorama the sky is baked into is a stored image and has nothing to do with a camera. If a readout does not hand over the raw value, none of them can be trusted.

decisions.title: The divide-by-clear-sky convention goes with it
decisions.why: It exists only so that brightening lands a sky value somewhere visible. Once nothing brightens the readout, it is a second unknown between the quantity and the pixel and buys nothing.

decisions.title: The seven brightness readouts are measured at full precision, not squeezed into a picture
decisions.why: They have no ceiling and a picture does. The alternative is dividing them by a number somebody chose, which is the habit we are removing. Reading them before they become a picture costs a small opening onto something the app already computes, and gives real brightness units instead of grey.

decisions.title: A car standing in front of a sky readout stops looking like a photograph
decisions.why: Taking the camera away applies to the whole frame, not just the sky behind. The old behaviour was deliberate and is worth naming, but a readout that is half measurement and half photograph is what made the sky unreadable in the first place.

next.if_nothing: I take the two faults the clean readouts exposed, starting with the one that blocks the null test.
